rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses addresses those who followed and believed in him.
rows.anchor: وهم الذين اتبعوه وآمنوا به

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: After the magicians believed, six hundred thousand Israelites followed Moses.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (لما آمنت السحرة اتبع موسى ستمائة ألف من بني إسرائيل)،

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The Israelites complained that Pharaoh had resumed killing their sons, and Moses told them to seek God's aid and endure what was being done to them.
rows.anchor: (وذلك أنهم شكوا إلى موسى إعادة # قتل أبنائهم، فقال موسى: {استعينوا بالله واصبروا} على ما يفعل بكم).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses gives his people hope that God will transfer Pharaoh's land to them after Pharaoh and his people are destroyed.
rows.anchor: هذا إطماع من موسى قومه في أن يورثهم الله أرض فرعون وقومه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Inheritance here means giving something to a successor after its predecessor.
rows.anchor: وهو جعل الشيء للخلف بعد السلف

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The final outcome for those who fear God is Paradise in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (أي: الجنة لمن اتقى الله في الآخرة)

rows.speaker: غيره
rows.claim: Another reported interpretation takes the final outcome here to mean victory and triumph.
rows.anchor: وقال غيره: (العاقبة (¬3) هاهنا النصر والظفر)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An outcome is what an initial event leads to, for good or ill; when said to belong to someone, it denotes a good outcome.
rows.anchor: إلا أنه إذا قيل: العاقبة له فهو في الخير

rows.speaker: أبو الدرداء، عطاء عن ابن عباس، الزجاج
rows.claim: They explain asaf as intense anger; the passage cites 43:55 as evidence, and al-Zajjaj is said to prefer this view.
rows.anchor: فقيل الأسف: الشديد الغضب، وهو قول أبي الدرداء (¬2)، وعطاء عن ابن عباس (¬3) واختيار الزجاج

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba also prefers the anger sense, glossing the verb as making someone angry and becoming angry.
rows.anchor: واختاره ابن قتيبة أيضا فقال: (يقال: آسفني فأسفت أي: أغضبني فغضبت،

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، السدي، الحسن
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi, and al-Hasan explain asaf as grief; al-Kalbi gives the same sense.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس (¬7) والسدي (¬8) والحسن (¬9): (الآسف الحزين)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two senses are close: anger grows from grief and grief from anger, with the response depending on whether the disliked event comes from an inferior or superior.
rows.anchor: والقولان متقاربان (¬2)؛ لأن الغضب من الحزن؛ والحزن من الغضب،

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth distinguishes anger when a disliked event comes from someone below from grief when it comes from someone above and cannot be endured.
rows.anchor: ما قاله الليث: (الأسف في حال الحزن، وفي حال الغضب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A cited line says that the grieving person is akin to a person of anger, illustrating the closeness of the two states.
rows.anchor: فحزن كل أخي حزن أخو الغضب

rows.speaker: الأعشى
rows.claim: Al-A'sha uses asif for anger, picturing a man as if his severed hand were stained with blood.
rows.anchor: قال الأعشى: أرى رجلا منهم أسيفا كأنما

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Aisha called Abu Bakr an asif, an example of the word's grief sense.
rows.anchor: حديث عائشة -رضي الله عنها (¬2) - أنها قالت: إن أبا بكر رجل أسيف

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد
rows.claim: Abu Ubayd defines asif as one who is quick to grief and melancholy.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيد: (الأسيف: السريع الحزن والكآبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses was angry at his people for worshipping the calf and grieved because God had tested them.
rows.anchor: فعلى هذا كان موسى غضبان على قومه لأجل عبادتهم العجل {أسفا} حزينا لأن الله فتنهم،

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi specifically glosses asaf as grief over the calf worship.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: {أسفا} حزينا لعبادة العجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses says their conduct after his departure was bad; the verb describes acting in a successor's place in a way one likes or dislikes.
rows.anchor: أي: بئسما عملتم بعدي، يقال: خلفه بما يكره، وخلفه بما يحب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies their bad conduct as adopting the calf and disbelieving in God.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يريد: اتخاذهم العجل وكفرهم بالله)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Haste is proceeding before the proper time and is blameworthy, whereas speed merely means doing something in less time and is not blameworthy.
rows.anchor: معنى العجلة (¬5): المتقدم بالشيء قبل وقته، ولذلك صارت مذمومة، والسرعة غير مذمومة؛

rows.speaker: الفراء، الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Farra and al-Zajjaj distinguish عجلت الشيء, to precede it, from أعجلته, to urge it.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء (¬6) والزجاج (¬7): (يقال: عجلت الشيء إذا سبقته، وأعجلته أي: استحثثته).

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets God's matter as His appointed promise, which the people failed to wait for.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يعني: ميعاد ربكم فلم تصبروا له)

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says God's promise was the forty nights; they assumed Moses had died when he did not return after thirty.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن (¬1): (وعد ربكم الذي وعدتم من الأربعين ليلة، وذلك أنهم قدروا أنه مات لما لم يأت على رأس الثلاثين ليلة).

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: Ata interprets the phrase as their hastening God's anger.
rows.anchor: وقال عطاء (¬2): (يريد: تعجلتم سخط ربكم).

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says they hastened to worship the calf before God's command came to them.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: (أعجلتم بعبادة العجل قبل أن يأتيكم أمر من ربكم)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the tablets Moses threw as the tablets containing the Torah.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يريد: التي فيها التوراة)

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A prophetic report says that what one is told is unlike what one sees: though informed of the trial and holding the tablets, Moses threw them after seeing his people worship the calf.
rows.anchor: وروي أن النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم - قال: "يرحم الله أخي موسى ما المخبر كالمعاين،

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says Moses held Aaron by his forelock and hair with his right hand and his beard with his left.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: (بذؤابة أخيه، وشعره بيده اليمنى، ولحيته باليسرى)

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbari explains that Moses reproached Aaron for not reporting the people's grave apostasy, and seized him because he thought Aaron had failed God by staying behind; Aaron explained that the people nearly killed him, after which Moses's suspicion passed and he prayed for both.
rows.anchor: وهذا بين في قوله: {قال يا هارون ما منعك إذ رأيتهم ضلوا}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase ابن أم is read with either kasra or fatha on the mīm.
rows.anchor: {قال ابن أم} قرئ بكسر الميم وفتحها

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: For the kasra reading, al-Zajjaj treats the expression as a unified noun with a genitive attachment; in the vocative it loses the yāʾ, whose trace remains in the kasra.
rows.anchor: من (¬2) كسر الميم فقال الزجاج: (فإنه أضاف إلى نفسه

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra says frequent vocatives addressed to oneself commonly drop the yāʾ, with يا ابن أم and يا ابن عم as familiar exceptions; less common forms retain it.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: (وذلك أنه كثر في الكلام، فحذفت العرب منه الياء،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The yāʾ remains in less common expressions such as يا ابن أبي, and the source cites Abu Zubayd's verse with يا ابن أمي as the original form.
rows.anchor: وقد جاء يا ابن أمي بإثبات الياء على الأصل كقول أبي زبيد

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh compares retaining the original form here to the established form al-quswa, whose rejected original was used.
rows.anchor: قال سيبويه: (فهذا بمنزلة القصوى الذي استعمل فيه الأصل الذي رفض في غيره)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Basran and Kufan grammarians agree on the kasra analysis described above.
rows.anchor: وهذا الذي ذكرنا قول البصريين والكوفيين بلا اختلاف بينهما

rows.speaker: البصريون
rows.claim: For the fatha reading, Basrans make ابن and أم a single compound, like خمسة عشر.
rows.anchor: فمذهب البصريين (¬5) فيه أنهم جعلوا: ابن وأم شيئا واحدا نحو: خمسة عشر

rows.speaker: الكوفيون، الفراء
rows.claim: Kufans analyze the fatha like a singular vocative in forms such as يا حسرتا, effectively addressing the mother as يا أماه.
rows.anchor: الكوفيين أنهم # قالوا: يا ابن أم ويا ابن عم فنصبوا كما ينصب المفرد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers the Basran account: the fatha on ابن is like that in خمسة and that on أم like that in عشر.
rows.anchor: والصحيح قول البصريين، وهو أن الفتحة في ابن كالفتحة في خمسة

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The commentators say Aaron was Moses's full brother and that ابن أم was used to soften and appeal to him.
rows.anchor: (وكان هارون أخا موسى لأبيه وأمه، وإنما قال. {يا ابن أم} ليستعطفه عليه ويرققه)

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi glosses استضعفوني as they humiliated and overpowered me.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: (استذلوني وقهروني)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aaron says the people intended to kill him.
rows.anchor: وهموا أن {يقتلونني}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The enemies Aaron asks not to be made a source of rejoicing for are the calf worshippers.
rows.anchor: {فلا تشمت بي الأعداء} يعني: أصحاب العجل.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aaron asks Moses not to include him among the wrongdoers in his anger and punishment.
rows.anchor: أي: في موجدتك (¬5) علي، وعقوبتك لي لا تجعلني معهم

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says Moses asks forgiveness for his own wrongdoing, meaning how he acted toward Aaron, though Aaron was innocent and had not neglected to oppose the calf worshippers.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: (رب اغفر لي ذنبي أي: ما صنعت إلى أخي)

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: The people of rhetorical interpretation say Moses sought forgiveness for Aaron in case he had fallen short in opposing the calf worshippers, although no such shortcoming occurred.
rows.anchor: كأنه يقول: اغفر لأخي إن قصر في الإنكار، كذلك (¬3) قال أهل المعاني

rows.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ata, transmitting from Ibn Abbas, explains entering God's mercy as entering the spaciousness of His Garden.
rows.anchor: قال عطاء عن ابن عباس (¬5): (يريد: في سعة جنتك).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling God the Most Merciful reports His attribute and expresses the supplicant's strong hope that the request will succeed through God's mercy.
rows.anchor: لأن من هو {أرحم الراحمين} يؤمل منه الرحمة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second object of اتخاذ is omitted: they took the calf as a god and object of worship, as 20:88 makes explicit.
rows.anchor: أن المفعول الثاني من مفعولي الاتخاذ محذوف على تقدير: اتخذوا العجل إلها (¬7) ومعبودا،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One of the two exegetical approaches identifies those who took the calf as the people who directly worshipped it.
rows.anchor: أحدهما: أن المراد بالذين اتخذوا العجل: الذين باشروا عبادة العجل

rows.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ata from Ibn Abbas says the wrath reached the calf worshippers in this world; they were pardoned through killing themselves and so do not incur this wrath in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: قال عطاء عن ابن عباس: (يريد: في الدنيا)

rows.speaker: أبو العالية
rows.claim: Abu al-Aliyah identifies the worldly wrath as the command that they kill themselves.
rows.anchor: قال: (هو ما أمروا به من قتلهم أنفسهم)

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says their humiliation came when they realized they had gone astray.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: (الذلة لحقتهم بأنهم رأوا أنهم قد ضلوا فذلوا)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the wrath and humiliation had already occurred, the future tense reports what God told Moses about his people after their calf worship; an implicit 'We said to Moses' is understood.
rows.anchor: هو أن هذه الآية إخبار

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، عطية العوفي
rows.claim: The second approach takes those who took the calf to mean their descendants who lived in the Prophet's time.
rows.anchor: أن المراد بالذين اتخذوا العجل أبناؤهم الذين كانوا في زمن النبي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the addressed people were those who encountered the Prophet, while their fathers had worshipped the calf; their coming wrath is Hereafter punishment and their worldly humiliation is the jizya.
rows.anchor: {سينالهم غضب}: (عذاب في الآخرة)

rows.speaker: العوفي
rows.claim: Al-Awfi says the descendants contemporary with the Messenger faced wrath and humiliation in the fate of Banu Qurayza and al-Nadir: killing and expulsion.
rows.anchor: وقال العوفي: (أراد سينال أولادهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation is that Arabs attribute ancestors' disgraceful deeds to descendants, as they also attribute ancestors' honors to them; the verse reproaches the Prophet-era Jews for their ancestors' calf worship.
rows.anchor: أن العرب تعير الأبناء بمعاير الآباء وتنسبها إليهم، كما تفعل ذلك في المناقب

rows.speaker: عطية العوفي
rows.claim: An alternative is ellipsis of a genitive: the original calf worshippers are named, but their children are the ones who will receive the wrath and humiliation.
rows.anchor: أن الآية من باب حذف المضاف على ما ذكره عطية العوفي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says God similarly punishes whoever takes a deity besides Him or turns to someone other than Him.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يريد: كذلك أعاقب من اتخذ إلها من دوني أو تولى غيري)

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: The people of rhetorical interpretation generalize the threat to every religious fabricator, whose recompense is God's wrath and worldly humiliation; they cite Malik on innovators bearing humiliation.
rows.anchor: وقال أهل المعاني: (كل مفتر في دين الله فجزاؤه غضب الله والذلة في الدنيا،

rows.speaker: مالك بن أنس
rows.claim: Malik is reported to say that every religious innovator bears humiliation above his head, and the passage applies this to the verse's fabricator.
rows.anchor: ما من مبتدع إلا وهو يجد فوق رأسه ذلة، ثم قرأ هذه الآية

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets the sins as shirk and links the wording to 4:18.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس (¬5): (يريد: الشرك، مثل قوله في النساء:

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says repentance means turning away from and abandoning those sins before punishment arrives and before death.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يعني: قبل حلول العذاب وقبل الموت).

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains believing as affirming that God alone is deity and has no partner.
rows.anchor: قال: (يريد: صدقوا أنه لا إله غيري ولا شريك معي)

rows.speaker: المفسرون، أهل اللغة
rows.claim: Commentators and linguists explain 'the anger became silent' as 'it subsided'; sakata can mean stillness or withholding, while samata specifically means closing the mouth against speech.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون (¬2)، وأهل اللغة (¬3): (أي: سكن)، والسكوت أصله السكون والإمساك عن الشيء،

rows.speaker: أصحاب النظر
rows.claim: The theorists explain the metaphor: anger's surge speaks for the inward state, so its calming is like the speaker falling silent.
rows.anchor: لما كان بفورته (¬6) دالا على ما في النفس للمغضوب عليه، كان بمنزلة الناطق بذلك،

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima reverses the construction, taking it to mean that Moses fell silent from anger, as when one says he put the cap into the head.
rows.anchor: وقال عكرمة: (المعنى: سكت موسى عن الغضب)

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq prefers the first interpretation, that the anger subsided, which he identifies as the Arab grammarians' view.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: (والقول الأولى، الذي معناه: سكن، وهو قول أهل العربية)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses picked up the tablets because he had thrown them down earlier.
rows.anchor: {أخذ الألواح}؛ لأنه كان قد ألقاها.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nuskha is writing a text from another text letter for letter; the source text and the copy are both called a nuskha because one stands in place of the other.
rows.anchor: وهو: اكتتابك كتابا عن كتاب حرفا بحرف، تقول: نسخته وانتسخته

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، عمرو بن دينار
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Amr ibn Dinar report that the tablets broke when Moses threw them; after a forty-day fast they were restored with the contents of the first tablets.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس (¬6) وعمرو بن دينار (¬7): (لما ألقى موسى الألواح تكسرت، فصام أربعين يوما،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the report that the tablets broke, their nuskha means what was copied from them.
rows.anchor: فعلى هذا معنى: {وفي نسختها}. أي: فيما (¬9) نسخ منها،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the same tablets remained intact, nuskha instead means their written contents, which were copied from an original.
rows.anchor: وإن كانت الألواح لم تتكسر، وأخذها موسى بعينها بعد ما ألقاها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وغيره
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and others gloss guidance as guidance from error and mercy as deliverance from punishment.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس (¬1) وغيره (¬2): (هدى من الضلالة، ورحمة من العذاب).

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains those who fear for their Lord as those who fear their Lord.
rows.anchor: يريد: الخائفين من ربهم

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisa'i says the prefixed object makes the lām natural, citing an older usage such as 'to you I honored' that is no longer common.
rows.anchor: فقال الكسائي: (8) تقدم المفعول على الفعل حسنت اللام)

rows.speaker: النحويون
rows.claim: The grammarians explain the lām as marking a fronted object whose precedence weakened the verb's government.
rows.anchor: قال النحويون: (لما تقدم المفعول ضعف عمل الفعل فيه، فصار بمنزلة ما لا يتعدى،

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
rows.claim: Abu Ali al-Farisi, representing most grammarians, treats the preposition as an added reinforcement with a transitive verb; he compares other constructions and 93:72.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو علي الفارسي -وهو قول أكثر النحويين-: (قد يزاد بحروف الجر في المفعول،

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another explanation takes the lām as purposive: they fear for their Lord, sincerely rather than for show.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم: إنها (¬4) لام أجل، والمعنى: هم (¬5) لأجل ربهم (¬6) {يرهبون}. لا رياء ولا سمعة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ikhtara derives from khayr and means to take the best; its original ya changed to alif after becoming vocalized following a fatḥa, accounting for forms such as mukhtar.
rows.anchor: الاختيار: افتعال من لفظ الخير، يقال: اختار الشيء أي: أخذ خيره وخياره

rows.speaker: جماعة النحويين
rows.claim: A group of grammarians reads the construction as 'Moses chose from his people,' with min omitted and the verb made directly transitive; they cite al-Farazdaq.
rows.anchor: قال جماعة النحويين (¬1): (معناه: واختار موسى [من] (¬2) قومه، فحذفت (من) ووصل الفعل فنصب،

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra says direct object use is allowed because min can be replaced by an annexation without changing the meaning of 'the best of the people.'
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: (وإنما استجيز وقوع الفعل عليهم إذا طرحت (من)؛

rows.speaker: الراعي
rows.claim: Al-Ra'i's verse says 'choose her a fat she-camel,' with 'from them' understood though min is omitted.
rows.anchor:
وأنشد للراعي (¬6):
فقلت (¬1) له (¬2) اخترها قلوصا سمينه

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu Ali states the general rule that verbs taking a second object through a preposition may drop that preposition, as in choosing from men, seeking forgiveness for a sin, and commanding someone to do good; he cites poetry for the pattern.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي: (والأصل في هذا الباب أن من الأفعال ما يتعدى إلى المفعول الثاني بحرف جر،

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says God instructed Moses to bring Israelites who would apologize for calf worship; Moses selected seventy to apologize at the appointed meeting.
rows.anchor: قال السدي: (أمر الله موسى أن يأتيه (¬3) [في] ناس من بني إسرائيل يعتذرون إليه من عبادة العجل،

rows.speaker: ابن يسار
rows.claim: Ibn Yasar says the seventy were chosen to repent for their deed and ask forgiveness on behalf of those who remained among their people.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن يسار (¬5): (اختارهم ليتوبوا إليه مما صنعوا، ويسألوه التوبة على (¬6) من ورائهم من قومهم)

rows.speaker: وهب
rows.claim: Wahb says they doubted that Moses heard God's speech and asked to hear it themselves so they could believe and remove suspicion.
rows.anchor: وقال وهب: (إنهم لم يصدقوا موسى أنه يسمع كلام الله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas takes the earthquake to mean that the seventy died.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يريد: ماتوا)

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj defines rajfa as violent motion and says the mountain shook them so they died.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: (والرجفة الحركة الشديدة، يقال: إنهم رجف بهم الجبل فماتوا)

rows.speaker: ابن يسار، السدي
rows.claim: Ibn Yasar and al-Suddi say the quake came after the people requested to see God openly (4:153).
rows.anchor: قال ابن يسار، والسدي: (إنما أخذتهم الرجفة لأنهم قالوا: {أرنا الله جهرة})

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another report from Ibn Abbas says they prayed for a privilege never given to anyone before or after them, which God disliked and answered with the quake.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: (إنهم قالوا في دعائهم: اللهم أعطنا ما لم تعطه أحدا قبلنا

rows.speaker: أبو الجوزاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Abu al-Jawza transmitting from Ibn Abbas says the quake came because the seventy had failed to forbid calf worship.
rows.anchor: وروى أبو الجوزاء (¬6) عنه قال: (إنما أخذتهم الرجفة لأنهم كانوا [لم] (¬7) ينهوا عن عبادة العجل)

rows.speaker: قتادة، ابن جريج، القرظي
rows.claim: Qatada, Ibn Jurayj, and al-Qurazi likewise say the seventy did not leave their people during calf worship or enjoin right and forbid wrong.
rows.anchor: ونحو ذلك قال قتادة وابن جريج (¬9) والقرظي (¬10) قالوا: (إنهم لم # يزايلوا قومهم حين عبدوا العجل،

rows.speaker: وهب
rows.claim: Wahb says the quake was not death but terror and shaking so severe that their joints nearly separated and their backs weakened; Moses feared they would die and prayed, and God removed the shaking.
rows.anchor: وقال وهب: (لم تكن تلك الرجفة موتا , ولكن القوم لما رأوا تلك الهيبة أخذتهم الرعدة

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj interprets Moses as saying that God could have killed them before testing them with the event that caused the quake.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: (أي: لو شئت أمتهم من قبل أن تبتليهم بما أوجب عليهم الرجفة)

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says Moses feared returning to Israel with its best men dead and no one to corroborate him; God then revived them.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: (قال موسى: يا رب كيف أرجع إلى بني إسرائيل وقد أهلكت خيارهم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses feared Israel would suspect him and not believe the seventy had died, so he asked why God had not destroyed them all, including him, before the meeting when Israel could witness it.
rows.anchor: أن موسى خاف أن يتهمه بنو إسرائيل على السبعين إذا عاد إليهم

rows.speaker: الفراء، الكلبي وجماعة
rows.claim: Al-Farra, al-Kalbi, and others say Moses thought the quake killed them for the calf worship, but the actual cause was their demand to see God (4:153).
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: (ظن موسى # أنهم أهلكوا باتخاذ [أصحابه] (¬1) العجل،

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbari rejects the idea that Moses thought God punished people for others' sins; he reads the question as a rhetorical denial, 'You would not destroy us for the fools' deed,' and says Moses did not know the quake's actual cause.
rows.anchor: ابن الأنباري (¬7) , [و] (¬8) على هذا أنكر موسى

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad reads the question as an appeal meaning, 'Do not destroy us.'
rows.anchor: قال المبرد: (هذا استفهام استعطاف أي: لا تهلكنا)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun 'it' refers back to the trial: the fools' lapse was God's testing, by which He misled some and guided others; this supports Moses's plea not to destroy them for their act.
rows.anchor: إن تلك الفتنة] (¬1) التي وقع فيها السفهاء لم تكن {إلا فتنتك} أي: اختبارك، وابتلاؤك،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author calls the verse manifest proof against the Qadariyya, leaving them no excuse.
rows.anchor: وهذه الآية من الحجج الظاهرة على القدرية التي لا يبقى لهم معها عذر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Write here means prescribe or make obligatory; asking for good in both lives parallels the believers' prayer in 2:201.
rows.anchor: أي: أوجب لنا، والكتابة تذكر بمعنى الإيجاب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets the worldly good as accepting their deputation and sending them back forgiven and shown mercy.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في الآية في هذه السورة: (يريد: اقبل وفادتنا وردنا بالمغفرة والرحمة)،

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the good in the Hereafter means Paradise, with the implied word 'good' repeated after 'and in the Hereafter.'
rows.anchor: {وفي الآخرة}، قال: (يريد: حسنة، يعني: الجنة)

rows.speaker: جميع المفسرين، أهل المعاني
rows.claim: All commentators and the people of rhetorical interpretation explain hudna as repenting and returning to God.
rows.anchor: قال جميع المفسرين (¬1) وأهل المعاني (¬2): (تبنا ورجعنا إليك بتوبتنا).

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth glosses hud as repentance.
rows.anchor: قال الليث: (الهود التوبة)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets God's punishment as striking someone for even a minor sin.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يريد: على الذنب اليسير)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's mercy means His willing good; every worldly or otherworldly good anyone receives is part of that mercy, some broader and some more particular.
rows.anchor: أن رحمة الله تعالى إرادته الخير (¬6)، وإرادته الخير تنقسم إلى أقسام كثيرة،

rows.speaker: الحسن، قتادة
rows.claim: The author prefers Hasan and Qatada's view: mercy embraces righteous and wicked people in this world but is reserved for the God-fearing in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: والأحسن في تفسير هذه الآية ما ذهب إليه الحسن وقتادة

rows.speaker: عطية العوفي
rows.claim: Atiyya al-Awfi explains that disbelievers receive provision and protection through believers because of God's mercy toward believers, but in the Hereafter mercy belongs to believers alone, like a person warmed by another's lamp.
rows.anchor: إن الكافر يرزق ويدفع عنه بالمؤمن لسعة رحمة الله للمؤمن

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj also chooses the interpretation that mercy embraces everyone in this world and the believers alone in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: وهذا اختيار الزجاج

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbari's first explanation takes mercy as God's beneficence, from which neither believer nor disbeliever is ever free, like rain called mercy.
rows.anchor: أن الرحمة يراد بها الصنع والأفضال، وما يخلو من صنع الله وأفضاله مؤمن ولا كافر

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: His second explanation limits 'everything' to all things eligible and deserving of mercy, just as 'everything' can mean everything possible for a particular recipient (6:44; 27:23).
rows.anchor: (أن رحمته (¬4) تسع كل شيء يجوز أن يدخل فيها، وأن يكون مستحقا لها

rows.speaker: جماعة المفسرين
rows.claim: A group of commentators describes the wording as a general expression intended to refer to a specific subset.
rows.anchor: وهذا مذهب جماعة المفسرين (¬1)، وهو أنهم قالوا: هذا من العام الذي أريد به (¬2) الخاص)
